A.coverage: Moderate coverage. It consistently identified the brick rowhouse façade, covered porch, weathered porch ceiling, security bars, concrete stairs, handrail, downspout, doors/windows, basement opening, and lawn. It was less detailed about surface wear and site clutter.
missing_visible_conditions: Satellite dish on the upper façade
Overhanging tree branches obscuring the upper elevation
Porch furniture and stored-item clutter
Visible wear, dirt, and discoloration on stair treads and sidewalls
Uneven lawn edge and lack of defined planting beds
Weathered upper cornice detailing
A.systematic_patterns: Usually grounded in large visible features. Repeated unsupported comparative-age claims about the stairs and one unsupported claim about replacement-window ages. Subjective curb-appeal language was occasionally stronger than the image alone can establish.
A.verbosity_bias: Concise; no penalty warranted. Claims generally stayed at feature-level rather than multiplying minor finish observations.

B.coverage: Very high coverage of visible renovation-relevant conditions. Across repeats it addressed nearly every visible exterior component, including brick, cornice, porch soffit and fascia, metalwork, bars, door, windows, porch contents, stairs, rail, lower masonry, basement window, drainage, dish, lawn, walkway, neighboring edges, and tree cover.
missing_visible_conditions: The unusually long and steep stair run as a circulation characteristic
The fact that only one central handrail is visible along the main stair run
B.systematic_patterns: Strong visual coverage but frequent over-resolution of fine details. It repeatedly asserted subtle corrosion, coating deterioration, dust, hardware age, and paint wear that are not always discernible at this image scale. Styling and broad discoloration claims were usually supported; actual age, causation, and fine material-condition claims were more often uncertain.
B.verbosity_bias: Extremely granular and repetitive; no penalty warranted. Many single visible conditions were restated as wear, discoloration, and dated-style claims.

A.coverage: Moderate-to-good coverage of the major visible layout and finish conditions. Across repeats it consistently captured the narrow aisle, compact work surfaces, raised-panel cabinetry, open shelving, backsplash/counter contrast, basic lights, patterned floor, ceiling discoloration, and rear clutter/storage.
missing_visible_conditions: Exposed bulbs or apparent missing diffuser at the front ceiling fixture
Visible scuffs/marks along the lower left wall and baseboard
The sink-side dish rack substantially obscuring the counter and sink
Irregular backsplash termination and transitions
A.systematic_patterns: A was strongest on layout, style, and broad modernization observations. It repeatedly overreached on functional conclusions such as two-person usability, storage inadequacy, and rear underutilization. Exact flooring material and assertions of wear were less certain than stated, and externally vented hood status was a hidden-system inference.
A.verbosity_bias: Concise to moderate. It generally grouped conditions rather than generating many minute surface-condition claims.

B.coverage: Very high coverage of nearly every visible surface and fixture, including ceiling, lights, walls, trim, baseboards, floor, cabinets, shelves, hood, counters, backsplash, sink, faucet, range, curtains, openings, and rear storage.
missing_visible_conditions: No dedicated under-cabinet task lighting is visibly installed
The sink and range leave only compact work/landing areas
B.systematic_patterns: B consistently captured visible objects and broad dated styling, but repeatedly overstated subtle grime, staining, wear, spotting, yellowing, and misalignment that the image does not clearly resolve. It also frequently treated the countertop's natural speckled pattern as staining or laminate wear and the floor's mottled pattern as damage. Negative claims scoped to clearly visible surfaces were often supportable, while claims about concealed areas, active failure, operation, or absent components were not.
B.verbosity_bias: Extremely granular and repetitive, often splitting one visible condition into several closely related claims. Verbosity itself was not penalized, but it produced many weakly evidenced micro-condition assertions.

A.coverage: Very high coverage of visible renovation-relevant conditions across ceiling panels/grid, exposed utilities, wiring, masonry walls, rear door, concrete floor, perimeter finishes, and clutter. It also inventories many movable contents that are not central renovation conditions.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong recognition of the damaged/misaligned suspended ceiling, exposed piping, rough painted masonry, worn door, stained slab, and clutter. Recurring overreach includes moisture interpretations, claims of looseness or inadequate support, hidden electrical/connection condition, temporal neglect, dust at low resolution, and misidentifying the red work light as a fan in repeat 2.
A.verbosity_bias: Extremely verbose and repetitive, repeatedly splitting the same visible condition into defect, degradation, age, dirt, and modernization formulations.

B.coverage: Moderate-to-good concise coverage of the low damaged ceiling, exposed plumbing/ducting, electrical panel, painted masonry discoloration, unfinished slab, and clutter. It captures the main room-level conditions but omits much of the detailed deterioration.
missing_visible_conditions: Worn and irregular rear door/jamb finishes
Rough, patched, and chipped wall coatings
Visible gaps and damaged edges in the rear door surround
Broad floor staining, scuffs, and rough perimeter transitions
Loose or deteriorated overhead pipe wrapping/insulation
Hanging or unorganized rear-ceiling cables
Leaning unfinished plywood sheet
B.systematic_patterns: Consistently identifies low headroom, patchwork or sagging ceiling materials, exposed services, wall staining, painted masonry, and the bare slab. It generally avoids causal moisture claims, but repeat 3 incorrectly infers no finished exits despite a visible rear door and cannot establish absence of windows outside the frame.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and selective, with little duplication compared with A.

A.coverage: Good coverage of the principal visible renovation conditions: narrow one-wall layout, limited counters, mixed cabinetry, damaged foreground cabinet/counter edge, open shelving, basic hood and light, wall scuffs, worn resilient flooring, register, and flooring transition.
missing_visible_conditions: Darkened, residue-marked range-hood filter/underside
Chipped and scuffed right doorway trim
The visible black freestanding range itself
A.systematic_patterns: Usually grounded in major visible features. It occasionally adds subjective age labels or function judgments, and one repeat improperly attributes cabinet wear to water. Ceiling staining and natural-light claims are also more speculative than the image allows.
A.verbosity_bias: Concise to moderate. It generally groups related visible conditions rather than repeatedly subdividing them.

B.coverage: Very high coverage of nearly every visible renovation-relevant surface and fixture, including cabinetry, damaged counter edging, shelving, backsplash, hood/filter, walls, trim, flooring, threshold, lighting, register, sink zone, range, and corridor layout.
B.systematic_patterns: Strong at locating small visible defects, especially the foreground cabinet/counter damage, wall marks, dirty hood filter, trim wear, and flooring condition. Systematically overstates age, grime, staining, appliance wear, cabinet misalignment, and ceiling discoloration where lighting, material pattern, or resolution make those details ambiguous. It also makes several absence or hidden-condition claims about structure, leaks, and operation that a single photo cannot verify.
B.verbosity_bias: Extremely granular and repetitive, splitting the same cabinet, counter, wall, trim, and flooring conditions into many overlapping claims. Verbosity itself was not used in claim grading.

A.coverage: Good concise coverage of the principal visible renovation conditions: severe vanity finish failure, dated tub/shower enclosure and surround, tight layout, older lighting/medicine cabinet, wall/trim wear, and window adjacency.
missing_visible_conditions: Visible gray discoloration and residue inside the tub
Broad uneven beige-gray ceiling discoloration
Bunched patterned window curtain
Dark marks around the toilet and lower wall/baseboard
Specific exposed dark substrate on the vanity was not consistently identified
A.systematic_patterns: Consistently identifies the major dated finishes and vanity damage. Repeatedly overreaches on vanity swelling and infers exhaust-fan absence from incomplete visibility. Some subjective layout observations are accurate but not defects by themselves.
A.verbosity_bias: Concise to moderate; generally groups related conditions rather than itemizing every surface.

B.coverage: Very high coverage of nearly every visible component and finish, including tub, surround, enclosure, vanity, sink, faucet, toilet, flooring, walls, ceiling, window, curtain, trim, switch, mirror, and lighting.
missing_visible_conditions: Tight spacing with the toilet positioned between the vanity and tub
The shower enclosure's strong visual obstruction of the narrow room
B.systematic_patterns: Strong at capturing visible aging, discoloration, and severe vanity finish loss. Frequently over-specifies exact materials, grime, mineral buildup, countertop haze, curtain wear, and grout where resolution is insufficient. It also occasionally adds unsupported causes or hidden-condition conclusions, especially water-related staining, active-leak implications, and overall functionality.
B.verbosity_bias: Extremely granular and repetitive, often restating the same condition with minor wording changes; verbosity itself does not affect claim labels.

A.coverage: Moderate. Across repeats it consistently captured the low/obstructed ceiling, damaged and discolored panels, exposed mechanicals and wiring, support post, concrete floor, sink, stairs, and clutter. It gave little attention to wall, floor, sink, and lighting surface condition.
missing_visible_conditions: Bare-bulb utilitarian lighting
Rough, marked, and inconsistently finished masonry walls
Loose or irregular rear-right wall covering
Visible floor staining, dirt, and surface wear
Visible grime and wear on the utility sink
A.systematic_patterns: Strong consistency on ceiling damage, exposed utilities, and low headroom. Repeatedly inferred that equipment or infrastructure was aging/dated without visually verifiable age and occasionally made condition judgments such as slab serviceability or an open drain without clear evidence.
A.verbosity_bias: Concise and selective; no grading penalty for brevity.

B.coverage: Very high. Across repeats it covered nearly every major visible renovation-relevant condition: ceiling deformation and openings, discoloration, exposed framing and utilities, walls, slab, sink, furnace/ducts, wiring, lighting, stairs, support post, rear wall covering, and clutter.
B.systematic_patterns: Excellent visible-condition breadth, but repeatedly decomposed the same surfaces into overlapping claims. It often overstated visually unverifiable age, dust, wear, support adequacy, maintenance history, or deferred upkeep. Claims limited to visible appearance were generally supported; historical, causal, and hidden-condition interpretations were often uncertain or unsupported.
B.verbosity_bias: Highly granular and repetitive; no grading penalty for verbosity.

A.coverage: Very high coverage. Across repeats A identified nearly all visible renovation-relevant exterior conditions: weathered/discolored masonry and joints, cornice soiling, aged window finishes, dirty basement openings and grilles, security-door wear, deteriorated concrete steps and landing, worn/corroded rail, cracked paving, weeds, and adjacent-entry deterioration.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong condition coverage but recurrent overreach on absence claims, especially no cracking, breakage, or structural failure. It also occasionally inferred moisture causation from generic dark staining and overstated ambiguous gaps or grille deformation. No claims were cost-bearing because every priced list was empty.
A.verbosity_bias: Highly granular and repetitive, frequently restating the same condition as aging, weathering, discoloration, and dated appearance. Verbosity itself did not affect claim grading.

B.coverage: Moderate coverage. B consistently captured the stone façade, arched openings, projecting bay, replacement/different windows, worn steps and landing, basic or worn rail, security door, and basement grilles. It was accurate but much less condition-specific than A.

B.systematic_patterns: B generally avoided hidden-system, moisture, structural, and safety speculation. Its main uncertainty came from unsupported provenance or subjective wording such as original, historic, attractive, and mismatched. No claims were cost-bearing because every priced list was empty.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and feature-oriented, with little repetition. It often named components without describing their visible deterioration.

A.coverage: Very high coverage. Across repeats, A identified the severe uneven and worn plank floor, wall stains and patches, damaged opening trim, ceiling irregularities, door and baseboard wear, fan, electrical covers, floor register, and visible kitchen elements.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong recall of nearly every visible surface. It sometimes over-specifies ambiguous details such as dust, grime, tarnish, exact patching, fan-blade damage, cabinet misalignment, hollow-core construction, and distant kitchen finish wear.
A.verbosity_bias: Highly granular and repetitive, often restating the same visible condition by defect, degradation, color, and style. Verbosity itself was not penalized.

B.coverage: Good coverage of the dominant conditions: severe floor deformation, wall and ceiling discoloration/patching, rough opening trim, dated fixtures and kitchen elements, worn door trim, and the narrow spatial arrangement. Coverage is materially less detailed than A.
missing_visible_conditions: Extensive floor scratches, abrasions, and worn finish beyond deformation and gaps
Visible wall holes, punctures, and discrete scuff marks
Baseboard scuffs and irregular floor-to-wall edges
Decorative metal floor register and its surrounding uneven flooring
B.systematic_patterns: Consistently captures the largest defects but omits smaller trim, vent, and surface-wear details. It occasionally makes broader spatial or availability inferences, especially circulation effects, galley constraint, and sparse electrical devices; the sparsity claim is not supportable from the frame.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and grouped, with broad summary claims rather than component-by-component detail. Verbosity itself was not penalized.

A.coverage: Good coverage of the principal visible renovation conditions: cracked/patchy ceiling, damaged wall finish, worn window trim, heavily worn flooring, loose cabling, aged/damaged fan, and worn baseboards. Coverage is materially less detailed than B but captures most major line-item conditions.
missing_visible_conditions: Severely broken or width-missing ceiling-fan blade was not consistently identified as a distinct visible condition until repeat 3.
Bent/uneven small-window mini-blind and absent covering at the larger window were not clearly covered across the prompt.
Visible shelf brackets/small shelf boards and their surrounding mounting damage were largely omitted.
Visible chipped/worn door edge and dull brass-colored knob were omitted.
Right-side partition/ledge paint wear was omitted.
A.systematic_patterns: Reliably identifies floor wear, ceiling cracking, wall marks, old windows, trim wear, loose cable, and old fan. It sometimes overreaches from discoloration to possible water staining and from the number of visible receptacles to limited outlet provision. Electrical-system condition is also inferred more strongly than the image supports.
A.verbosity_bias: Concise to moderate; combines related defects into broader claims without excessive repetition.

B.coverage: Very high visible-condition coverage, including ceiling cracks and patching, broken fan blade, fan finish, extensive wall damage, windows and blind, flooring, baseboards, shelving, partition, door, and loose cables. Nearly every visible renovation-relevant area is mentioned in each repeat.
B.systematic_patterns: Strong and consistent at localized visual inventory, especially the ceiling, fan blade, walls, floor, trim, blind, and cable locations. Recurrent overreach includes asserting dust/grime where only darkening is resolvable, calling shelves absent despite visible small boards, labeling the right partition as a stair enclosure, asserting functionality from missing coverings, and assigning cable or flooring type beyond what the photo can establish.
B.verbosity_bias: Extremely granular and repetitive, often splitting one visible condition into several overlapping claims; verbosity itself does not affect evidentiary grading.

A.coverage: Good coverage of the principal visible renovation conditions: dated and worn cabinets, range, counters, flooring, damaged walls, discolored ceiling, window/door wear, open cabinet bay, floor register, and exposed under-counter cabling. Coverage was less detailed than B but generally captured the major line-item conditions.
missing_visible_conditions: Microwave installed in an open upper-cabinet cubby
Partially visible white refrigerator/appliance at right
Missing lower-right cabinet door/front was not explicitly identified as missing, only described as open
Minimal or absent finished backsplash treatment
Dingy or uneven window blinds, valance, and curtain condition
A.systematic_patterns: Generally reliable on major visible conditions. Repeatedly treated counter material as definite laminate despite limited visual certainty, sometimes characterized visible cables as exposed electrical wiring, and made unsupported space/capacity judgments such as limited pantry or counter space. Flooring material varied between painted plank, sheet, and vinyl across repeats.
A.verbosity_bias: Moderate and concise. It emphasizes broad renovation categories rather than cataloging every small surface mark.

B.coverage: Very high coverage of nearly every visible renovation-relevant condition, including ceiling discoloration, wall damage, trim wear, worn plank flooring, register, open-framed left counter, cables, door and window treatments, range, cabinets, missing lower cabinet front, counters, sink, minimal backsplash, microwave cubby, and partial appliance edge.
B.systematic_patterns: Strong visual recall and broad coverage, with many supported observations. Recurring overreach involved asserting exact materials, causes of discoloration, actual component age, electrical/utility identity of cables, and subtle grime, fading, misalignment, or damage beyond the image resolution. Flooring material was inconsistent across repeats, and several ambiguous surfaces were labeled laminate or resilient/vinyl without definitive evidence.
B.verbosity_bias: Extremely granular and repetitive. The same visible condition is often restated as damage, wear, discoloration, age, and style in separate claims; this does not reduce evidentiary credit but makes the output inefficient.

A.coverage: Very high coverage. Across repeats A identified nearly all prominent visible renovation-relevant conditions: worn/discolored wood flooring and seams, marked and uneven wall paint, rough or missing lower trim, worn window trim, damaged or uneven blinds, aged fan, exposed ductwork with taped joints, loose wiring and mounting remnants, right-wall rack, worn door, outlet area, and floor cable.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong visible-condition recall, but recurrent overprecision about material, age, grime, texture, paint layers, wire type, and component usage. Ceiling discoloration was repeatedly stated despite strong lighting and shadow ambiguity. Some compound floor and blind claims combined clear wear with less-visible gouges, dust, or damage.
A.verbosity_bias: Highly granular and repetitive, often splitting one visible condition into several overlapping material, wear, color, and style claims. Verbosity itself was not penalized.

B.coverage: Moderate-to-high coverage of the major conditions. B consistently captured the exposed duct, worn flooring, marked paint, incomplete baseboards, loose wiring, aged fan/windows, and damaged blinds, but gave less detail on the worn door, right-wall rack, leaning panels, taped duct joints, window-sill damage, and outlet-area wear.
missing_visible_conditions: Scuffed and chipped lower door finish
Loose cable lying across the floor near the door/outlet
Leaning panels or trim pieces on the left
Right-wall projecting black metal shelf/rack wear and surrounding marks
Visible taped or wrapped duct joints
Specific worn/chipped window sill and lower-trim edges
B.systematic_patterns: Repeatedly introduced unsupported moisture interpretations from visible discoloration, inferred the age or abandonment of hidden electrical systems, and inferred too few outlets from incomplete room visibility. It reliably captured broad renovation issues but sometimes used speculative labels such as improvised ductwork, mismatched windows, patching, or painted flooring.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and aggregated, with fewer duplicative claims than A. Verbosity was not used as a grading factor.

A.coverage: Very high coverage. Across repeats it identifies nearly all visible renovation-relevant conditions: severely worn and irregular flooring, rough transitions, marked walls, missing wall plates, sparse base trim, ceiling seam/discoloration, older fixtures, stair/header finish issues, and damage to the black right-side surface.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong condition coverage, but repeatedly overstates fine details that are difficult to resolve, especially wear on every stair component, ceiling-plane unevenness, fan-blade alignment, component age, and the exact identity of the round ceiling fixture. It otherwise remains largely grounded in visible evidence.
A.verbosity_bias: Highly verbose and repetitive, often splitting one visible condition into many overlapping claims; verbosity itself was not penalized.

B.coverage: Good but less detailed coverage. It consistently captures the major floor damage, lower-wall marks, incomplete electrical plates, ceiling seam/discoloration, dated stair/fixtures, and constrained layout.
missing_visible_conditions: Heavy scuffing, scratching, dust, chipped edges, and worn finish on the large black right-side surface
Visible scratches and finish wear on stair treads and lower stair components
Scattered debris and pale speckling on the floor
B.systematic_patterns: Generally grounded, but compound shorthand sometimes mixes supported and unverified details, such as floor patching, rough baseboards, or limited lighting. One repeat introduces unsupported moisture as a possible cause of floor damage, and references to baseboards are imprecise because conventional baseboards are largely absent.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and selective, combining conditions into broader claims rather than enumerating every surface detail.

A.coverage: Very high coverage of visible renovation-relevant conditions. Across repeats it identifies the major wall-finish failure, holes and rough openings, exposed surface-run cable, striped paint, worn/marked floor, perimeter gaps, rough baseboards, worn door and trim, wall device, and older fan.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong recall but frequent over-description of ceiling unevenness, fan-shade mismatch, metal tarnish, exact wall/floor materials, fixture age, and hidden functionality. It generally performs best on direct wall, cable, trim, door, and floor observations.
A.verbosity_bias: Highly verbose and repetitive, often splitting one visible condition into several overlapping claims. Verbosity was not used as a grading factor.

B.coverage: High coverage of the principal renovation conditions, especially peeling paint, holes/scuffs, rough cable penetrations, exposed cable, dated fan, worn floor, rough trim, and door wear. It is less granular than A.
missing_visible_conditions: Small white wall-mounted device/plate near the right doorway and its rough surrounding paint

B.systematic_patterns: Usually anchors claims to prominent visible defects. Recurring weak points are calling small holes specifically nail/screw holes, describing floor discoloration as staining, and occasionally adding subjective spatial or age language. One repeat incorrectly calls the coordinated fan/light mismatched.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and condition-focused, with little duplication. Verbosity was not used as a grading factor.

A.coverage: Very high coverage of visible conditions: layout, wall damage, both partition openings, vanity-base failure, cabinetry, floor, toilet, accessories, countertop, sink, faucet, mirror, light, vent, curtain, electrical plate, and trim. Coverage was often repeated at very fine granularity.
A.systematic_patterns: Strong recurring detection of wall scuffs, open partition cutouts, missing vanity toe-kick, dated finishes, and dark floor/vanity marks. It systematically overinterpreted ambiguous appearance as wear, tarnish, corrosion, dust, mineral residue, countertop wear, or soiling; it also occasionally asserted material type such as drywall or structural material without direct support.
A.verbosity_bias: Highly verbose and repetitive, splitting single visible conditions into many overlapping styling, wear, discoloration, and condition claims. Verbosity itself was not penalized.

B.coverage: Good but less granular coverage of the major visible renovation conditions: narrow layout, central partition, upper opening, lower access panel, wall scuffs, damaged/open vanity base, dated finishes, ceiling fixtures, and floor. Some secondary conditions received little or no attention.

B.systematic_patterns: Consistently identified the narrow alcove, partition openings, wall scuffs, and open vanity base. It generally avoided the fine-grained tarnish and grime speculation seen in A, but sometimes used broad subjective labels such as dated, mismatched, low-grade, or worn. One repeat incorrectly inferred that no shower was visible despite the partial curtain, and another speculated about the floor being newer than other finishes.
B.verbosity_bias: Concise and broad, with relatively little duplication. Verbosity itself was not rewarded or penalized.
